name: navbar
description:
The bar at the top of every surface, and the most under-described unit in the system — it was two slots and three variants while the real header carried a fixed-over-hero mode, a sticky mode, a scroll-triggered glass-to-solid swap, a light/dark bar that depends on both, and a full-screen mobile menu, all of it written inline with `color-mix` and `backdrop-filter` in a `style` attribute. A composite of composites: it holds the logo, a set of nav-links, a set of buttons, and on a narrow viewport a drawer holding the same links rather than a second copy of them.

It collapses ON ITS OWN CONTAINER. Below 48rem of BAR width the links hide and the toggle appears; above it, the reverse. Neither depends on the viewport, so the same navbar behaves correctly in a phone, in a 400px preview card, and in a split pane — and the surface no longer has to tell it which of those it is in.

The drawer it opens is not part of this unit. `nav-menu` is a separate composite because the full-screen menu is `position: fixed` over the whole page and must escape this bar's `backdrop-filter` — a filtered ancestor creates a containing block for fixed descendants, so a menu nested inside a glass bar is trapped inside the bar. The real header already discovered this and renders the menu as a sibling.

base.transition: background var(--duration-moderate) var(--ease-out), border-color var(--duration-moderate) var(--ease-out)
base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

An explicit `display`, and it is load-bearing rather than tidy. `container-type: inline-size` has NO EFFECT on an element whose display is `inline` — containment needs a block box. This unit declared no display, so rendered as a `<span>` it was `inline`, its containment was inert, and every `@container` rule inside it silently never matched. The navbar found it: at 318px it was still showing a full desktop nav because the query it was waiting on could not fire.

bar.$description:
When the bar is narrow, EVERYTHING except the brand and the toggle goes. It was only the links: the social row and the language switch stayed, crowding a 320px bar beside a hamburger that offers the same things one tap away. The menu is where they live at that width — which is what the menu is for.

IT COLLAPSES IN TWO STAGES, because the things in it are not equally important. Below 62rem the social row and the language switch go — they are reachable in the menu and neither is why anyone came. Below 34rem the LINKS go too. Between those two widths, which is where a tablet sits, you get the navigation and the call to action and nothing else: the destinations survive longest because they are the bar's actual job.

One stage was wrong in both directions. At 768px it hid the nav — a tablet has room for four links — and at 400px it kept the social row beside a hamburger offering the same four marks one tap away.

The call to action SHRINKS with the bar. At full width it is the page's main affordance and earns its size; beside a hamburger on a 390px bar the same button is most of the row. It sets the button's own size properties rather than restating what `sm` means, so the two cannot drift apart.

links.$description:
Visible by DEFAULT, hidden when the bar is narrow. It was the other way round — `display: none` in the base, and a `breakpoint: md` variant that set `display: none` again. So the links were hidden always, the variant that claimed to hide them changed nothing, and the only thing ever revealing them was a surface writing its own rule. Three separate bugs agreeing with each other.

The threshold is measured, not chosen: brand 118px + links 360px + actions 128px + gaps needs 686px, so 48rem gives about 80px of headroom — which the German labels use, since MARKTPLATZ runs longer than MARKETPLACE.

Hidden on the BAR's width, not the window's. A navbar in a 400px preview card and a navbar on a 400px phone are the same problem; a viewport query gets the first one wrong, which is exactly what the storybook showed.

The LAST thing to go, at 34rem. The links are what a navigation bar is for, so they outlive the social row and the language switch by nearly thirty rem — a tablet keeps its navigation, a phone does not have room for it.

toggle.$description:
The inverse of `links`, on the same container width, so exactly one of the two is ever visible. Both were shown at once before — the desktop links AND the hamburger — which offers the same navigation twice and makes the hamburger look broken when pressing it reveals nothing new.

It appears the moment ANYTHING has been folded away — below 62rem, not below 34 — because that is when there is something behind it. A hamburger that opens a menu holding nothing the bar was not already showing is a control that teaches you to ignore it.

It does NOT push itself. `navbar-actions` carries the only auto margin, and the toggle sits immediately after it — so the call to action and the hamburger travel to the trailing edge as a pair. Both having `margin-inline-start: auto` split the free space between them and parked the button in the middle of the bar with a gap before the menu, which reads as two unrelated controls rather than one group.

drawer.$description: Full-height and translated off-screen rather than `display:none`, so it can animate and so focus management has something real to trap. It is `inert` while closed, which is what stops a keyboard from tabbing into a menu nobody can see.

overlay.$description: Fixed over a full-bleed hero, so the media sits behind it. The bar is transparent until the page scrolls; text over imagery is the one case where the page inks do not apply and the light ink is used throughout.

glass.$description: A translucent bar with a backdrop blur, for the scrolled state over content. The fill is a named tint rather than an inline `color-mix`, which is where this lived: in a `style` attribute, in one component, unthemeable. The blur radius is literal: there is no blur scale in this brand yet, and inventing a one-entry scale to hold a single value is worse than the value.

open.$description: The drawer arrives. The toggle keeps `aria-expanded` in step; the bar itself goes solid so the drawer does not appear to float over nothing.

reducedMotion.$description: The drawer still moves — removing the transform leaves it permanently off-screen — it just arrives instantly.

a11y.note: ONE `<nav>` with one label, in both layouts. The toggle is a real button carrying `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`; while the drawer is closed it must be `inert` or hidden, or a keyboard tabs into an invisible menu. Opening moves focus into the drawer, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the toggle. WCAG 2.4.11: a sticky bar must not cover a focused element, so anything focusable below it needs scroll-margin at least the bar's height.
